title: Effects of Hook Maneuver on Oxygen Saturation Recovery After ‒40 m Apnea Dive. A randomized Crossover Trial
content: Background: To reduce the risk of syncope, trained breath-hold divers (BHD) use a specialized breathing technique after surfacing called “hook breathing” (HB). It consists of a full inspiration followed with a valsalva-like maneuver and with subsequent exhalation performed against resistance to generate continuous positive airway pressure during exhalation. Aims: This study analysed the influence of HB on oxygen saturation recovery after ‒40 m depth apnea dive in trained BHDs. Methods: Thirteen BHDs performed two dives to ‒40 m at different days, one followed by using HB after dive and the other using Usual Breathing (UB). To detect signs of lung edema, ultrasound B-line measurements were conducted before, 10-min after the dive and within 1 hour after the dive. To detect oxygen saturation recovery, pulse oximetry were recorded before, and immediately after surfacing. Results: Both groups exhibited significant increases in SpO₂ over time (UB: F(2.25, 24.7) = 22.1, p &lt; 0.001, ηg2 = 0.612; HB: F(2.11, 23.2) = 29.0, p &lt; 0.001, ηg2 = 0.688). Significant differences in SpO₂ were observed between the HB and UB groups at 30–45 seconds post-apnea, with higher SpO₂ values in the HB group. 4 participants showed ultrasound B-lines within ten minutes post-dive. Conclusion: After 40-m apnea dive, the results revealed significant SpO₂ recovery from 30 seconds to 45 seconds, with the HB recovering more rapidly. No differences were found at earlier (10-25 seconds) or later time points (50-60 seconds). Further evidence should explore this phenomena with larger sample sizes.
